ROC-AUC, PR-AUC and time-dependent AUC (simple)
records.text: A score can put people in the right order while getting their numerical risks wrong. Good ranking alone does not show that using the score helps patients.

records.name: C-index (concordance index), Harrell's and Uno's (simple)
records.text: This measure checks whether predicted risk order matches observed event order. Unknown later outcomes need suitable handling.

records.name: Calibration: reliability diagrams and the Brier score (simple)
records.text: A risk estimate needs checking against what actually happens over the same time. A correct overall average can hide errors in lower- and higher-risk groups.

records.name: Positive predictive value (PPV) (simple)
records.text: Among people with a positive result, how many really meet the condition being tested? The answer depends on the test and the population.

records.name: Phase 1, 2 and 3 trials (simple)
records.text: Trial phases describe the questions being studied, such as dose, safety and treatment comparison. A phase number does not promise benefit or tell you how treatment is assigned.

records.name: Randomised trial (simple)
records.text: Chance assigns people to different treatment groups. This helps make a fair comparison, but does not guarantee identical groups or complete follow-up.

records.name: Preclinical (simple)
records.text: Laboratory and other model studies can help explain a treatment and guide human studies. A model response does not establish benefit for patients.

records.name: In vitro and in vivo (simple)
records.text: Check whether a result was measured in a laboratory, removed living tissue, a living animal or person, or a computer model. Each setting includes and leaves out different things.

records.name: N-of-1 trial (simple)
records.text: A planned comparison in one person may use repeated treatment periods. Lasting effects or changes over time can prevent a fair comparison.

records.name: Pre-specified vs post-hoc analysis (simple)
records.text: Find out what was planned before the relevant results were seen, and what was explored afterwards. Useful discoveries still need an appropriate later test.

records.name: Subgroup analysis (forest plots) (simple)
records.text: A treatment can be studied in groups defined by age, a marker or another feature. Different-looking results do not by themselves prove different treatment effects.

records.name: Group sequential design, stopping rules and alpha spending (simple)
records.text: A trial can plan checks before it finishes. The evidence needed at each check follows rules designed to account for repeated looks.

records.name: Futility analysis (stopped for futility) (simple)
records.text: A trial may stop because it is unlikely to meet its planned goal. That does not prove the treatments are equal.

records.name: Real-world evidence (simple)
records.text: Health records and other routinely collected data can answer useful questions. Why people received different care and when follow-up began still matter.

records.name: Publication format and peer-review status (simple)
records.text: Find the exact study report and version before using its result. A full paper, an early report and a correction can describe different stages of the same study.

records.name: Case report (simple)
records.text: A report of what happened to one person can raise useful questions. It usually cannot separate the treatment effect from other possible explanations.

records.name: Meta-analysis (simple)
records.text: A calculation that combines results from suitable studies. A precise average can still hide different results, bias or incompatible questions.

records.name: Controlled perturbation experiment (simple)
records.text: Change a defined factor and compare the result with suitable controls. A real change in a laboratory test does not by itself show why it happened or that patients benefit.

records.name: False discovery rate (simple)
records.text: A multiple-testing rule limits the expected share of false findings among selected results under stated assumptions. It does not tell you which individual finding is false.

records.name: Actionable genomic biomarkers (simple)
records.text: A DNA finding needs evidence for a particular treatment decision. A match to a gene or to another cancer is not enough on its own.

records.name: Detection and quantification limits (simple)
records.text: A test may find a signal before it can measure the amount reliably. Its limits belong to the stated method and sample conditions.

records.name: Prognostic and predictive biomarkers (simple)
records.text: A marker can describe the likely outcome or help identify a difference in treatment benefit. Those are different questions and need different comparisons.

records.name: Confounding by indication (simple)
records.text: People may receive different care because their health differs. Those starting differences can also affect the outcome.

records.name: Biomarker cutoff selection and validation (simple)
records.text: The line used to call a result positive needs its own evidence. A line chosen because it looked best in one set of results needs testing beyond those same results.
